name: Ubongo: educational cartoons for children in Africa (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Ubongo publishes no audience split by country; weighted to Tanzania, where it began and broadcasts most, then Kenya and Nigeria (its largest other markets) and the other countries whose languages it dubs into (Kinyarwanda, Chichewa and others), a judgment.
summary: Ubongo makes educational cartoons for TV, radio and online in Africa: Akili and Me for children of 3-6 (early literacy, numeracy, English, emotions) and Ubongo Kids for 7-14 (maths and science), broadcast free in about 22 countries; its US arm spent 7.2 million dollars in 2024 and Ubongo counts 42 million households reached a month, about 25 cents per child a year. Preschoolers in poor countries who watch Sesame Street's local versions at home learn about a fifth of a standard deviation more in a season, and Tanzanian children who watch Ubongo Kids score about 0.15 standard deviations higher in maths; we spread each gain over the years a child watches, cut it for occasional viewers, survey and small-study bias and fade-out, and value it as higher adult earnings. That gives about {{result}} years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, but the result is mostly uncertainty: the size of the home-viewing effect, how much of it lasts into adult earnings, and whether the audience counts are right drive it. The whole programme is discounted for missing data, as no controlled study measures Ubongo's home audience in standard deviations.

Households reached each month (TV, radio and online)

source.title: Ubongo, Strategic Plan 2024-2028
source.quote: Currently reaching 42 million households monthly on TV, radio and digital in 12 languages and 22 countries

rows.explainer: Ubongo's own count from media ratings and household surveys in its markets (p. 10: character recognition 'measured through nationally representative household surveys'), as of 2024. The unit is loose: the plan also says 'By 2024, we have reached 42 million kids' (p. 21), and the count includes radio-only listeners, whose dose is unknown. Taken as Ubongo states it; the doubt about who really watches, and how often, is in watch_share and implementation_adj.

rows.label: Average household size
rows.explainer: The site's household sizes for Ubongo's three largest markets (Tanzania, Kenya, Nigeria), about {{row:household_size}} people; Tanzania's figure is the rural one, the only one the site has. Households with a television are more often urban and smaller, so this is a little high.

rows.label: Share of household members aged 3-14 (the shows' audience)

source.title: World Bank, World Development Indicators: population ages 0-14 (% of total), 2024
source.quote: Tanzania 42.5, Kenya 36.8, Nigeria 41.0 (per cent of the population aged 0-14)

rows.explainer: About 40% of people in Tanzania, Kenya and Nigeria are 0-14 (World Bank, 2024); ages 3-14, the ages of Akili and Me (3-6) and Ubongo Kids (7-14), are about four fifths of that in a young population: 31%. Low 27% for urban, television-owning households with fewer children; high 34%.

rows.label: Share of children aged 3-14 in a reached household who watch or listen
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (35-70%): Ubongo counts households, and not every child in a household that tunes in watches: some are at school when the shows air, some are too old for Akili and Me or too young for Ubongo Kids. Anchor: the result, about 0.7 children per household, against Ubongo's own 'reached 42 million kids' (p. 21), which would be 1 per household.

rows.label: Children aged 3-14 who watch or listen in a month
rows.explainer: About 28 million children, counted as one year's audience against one year's cost; each is credited with one year of viewing's gain below.

rows.label: Learning gain of a preschooler who watches a season at home (standard deviations)

source.title: Mares & Pan (2013), Effects of Sesame Street: a meta-analysis of children's learning in 15 countries, Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology 34:140-151, doi:10.1016/j.appdev.2013.01.001 (open copy)
source.quote: The average effect estimate for surveys conducted in low- and middle-income countries was significant and positive (d = .213, SE = .070, 95% confidence interval = .076-.351, z = 3.04).

rows.explainer: Viewers against non-viewers (or heavy against light viewers) of a broadcast season of Sesame Street's local co-productions, in the six surveys in low- and middle-income countries where children chose to watch at home (29 estimates, 5,967 children, nearly all preschoolers): the Akili and Me audience, watching as they choose. The pooled d covers literacy and numeracy, world knowledge and social reasoning (Table 2), so those are in the earnings chain already. Studies where children were shown the programme find more (experiments 0.377 against surveys 0.262, Table 4), so there is no sign that home-viewing surveys run high. Ubongo's own trials point the same way: four weeks of daily Akili and Me improved Tanzanian pre-schoolers' scores on five of seven outcomes against children shown other programmes (Borzekowski 2018, Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology 54:53-59), a Rwanda trial on eight of ten (Borzekowski and others 2019, International Journal of Early Childhood 51:109-126, https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1215041), about 0.17 SD on average as Founders Pledge reads them (https://www.founderspledge.com/research/ubongo), while a northern Nigeria study found 'no differences associated with study's initial group assignments', with the control group exposed during the COVID-19 shutdown (Borzekowski and others 2023, https://www.ubongo.org/wp-content/uploads/Akili-and-Me-and-the-COVID-19-shutdown-1.pdf, p. 1). Those doubts are in evidence_adj.

rows.label: Share of the child audience aged 3-6 (Akili and Me)
rows.explainer: Judgment 36% (30-40%): ages 3-6 are 4 of the 12 years of the audience (3-14), a third, and in the young populations of Tanzania, Kenya and Nigeria each year of age is a slightly larger cohort than the one above it (World Bank, 2024: 37-43% of people are 0-14). Low 30% if older children watch more of the airtime; high 40% if preschoolers, at home in the day, watch more.

rows.label: Akili and Me: a preschooler's whole gain from all the years watched, relative to one season's
rows.explainer: Judgment 1.3 (1-2): the surveys measure one season, and later seasons repeat much of it (letters and counting once known); Ubongo's trials find about as much after four weeks of daily viewing (about 0.17 SD) as the surveys after a season (0.21), so the gain comes early and levels off. Low 1 if later years add nothing lasting; high 2 if each of the first two seasons teaches as much.

rows.label: Akili and Me: years a preschool viewer watches
rows.explainer: Judgment 2.5 years (1.5-4): the show is for ages 3-6, four years, but many children start late or stop when they start school. The audience is counted every year, so a year of viewing is credited with the whole gain over these years (one cohort a year, one gain).

rows.label: Akili and Me: gain credited to a year of viewing (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: A preschooler's whole gain over the years watched, divided by those years, so the audience counted every year adds up to one gain per child, never one per year.

rows.label: Ubongo Kids: gain of a 7-14-year-old who watches, after the years watched (standard deviations)

source.title: Watson (PhD thesis, Cambridge), educational television and learning in Tanzania (Ubongo Kids, Uwezo data); also Watson, Hennessy and Vignoles, British Journal of Educational Technology 52(2), 2021
source.page: Table 6.1, PDF p. 169 (printed p. 165); maths SD p. 209

rows.explainer: Tanzanian children who had watched Ubongo Kids in the past week against those who hadn't, in Uwezo's 2017 household survey (about 39,000 children aged 6-16): 0.126 on a maths scale whose SD is 0.841, 0.15 SD (SE 0.035/0.841, so 0.07-0.23 at 95%). The show had been on air since January 2014, so this is the difference after the years watched, not one season's. Cross-sectional: viewers may differ from non-viewers, which is in evidence_adj; the regression also holds Kiswahili attainment fixed, which the show may raise too. In the same regression a year of age, with its schooling, is worth 0.075 SD.

rows.label: Ubongo Kids: years a viewer had watched by the survey
rows.explainer: Judgment 3 years (2-4): Uwezo's survey was in 2017 and Ubongo Kids had been broadcast in Tanzania since January 2014, up to four years; a viewer in the past week had mostly watched for some of them. Divides the survey's gap to give a year of viewing's share.

rows.label: Ubongo Kids: gain credited to a year of viewing (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: The viewers' gap after the years watched, divided by those years: one gain per child over the years counted.

rows.label: Share of the learning gain still there in adult life
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for low- and middle-income countries (@education.test_gain_persistence_to_adulthood: {{row:learning_persistence}}, 20-70%): test gains fade between the programme and adult work.

rows.label: Adult earnings gain per SD of skill held as an adult
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for low- and middle-income countries (@education.earnings_gain_per_sd_adult_skills_lmic: {{row:earnings_gain_per_sd}}, 10-30%), per SD of reading and maths skill still there in adult life, so it multiplies the persisting share above. A cross-check: Kearney and Levine find more exposure to Sesame Street raised US children's chance of being at the right grade for their age (3.2 points for a 30-point rise in coverage), but no significant effect on attainment or wages; their small estimates are consistent with the test-score gains (NBER w21229, pp. 4, 24 and 28, https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w21229/w21229.pdf).

rows.label: Akili and Me: years from viewing to adult earnings
rows.explainer: Judgment 14 years (12-16): Akili and Me's viewers are 3-6, about 4.5 on average, and start earning at about 16-20.

rows.label: Ubongo Kids: years from viewing to adult earnings
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for primary-age audiences (@education.years_primary_programme_to_work: {{row:uk_years_to_work}} years): Ubongo Kids' viewers are 7-14.

rows.label: Years the earnings gain lasts
rows.explainer: The shared figure (@givewell_shared.long_term_benefit_years), as in every model of later income.

rows.label: Household members who share the earnings gain
rows.explainer: The shared figure (@givewell_shared.resource_sharing_multiplier): the earner's household shares the extra income, as in the later-income rows of every model.

rows.label: Consumption per person a year in Kenya, for reading (2021 PPP dollars)
rows.explainer: For reading only: the gain below is a share of the viewer's future earnings, so no baseline enters it. Kenya's household-survey mean, one of Ubongo's main markets, gives the scale: a 0.1% gain on it is about a dollar a year.

rows.label: Gain in ln(consumption) per child, over working life, discounted to today
rows.formula: (preschool_share * ln(1 + ak_gain_per_year_sd * learning_persistence * earnings_gain_per_sd) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - ak_years_to_work) + (1 - preschool_share) * ln(1 + uk_gain_per_year_sd * learning_persistence * earnings_gain_per_sd) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - uk_years_to_work)) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, working_years) * resource_sharing_multiplier
rows.explainer: For each show, ln(1 + a year of viewing's gain × share lasting into adult life × earnings per SD) in each working year, discounted at the shared rate after that show's wait until work; weighted by the audience's ages and shared with the household. Before the adjustments below.

rows.label: Learning by caregivers and others outside the counted audience, as a share of the children's benefit
rows.explainer: A side effect, judgment 5% (0-10%): children over 14 and adults in the household watch too, and Ubongo makes parenting content for caregivers. No study measures what they gain; they are a small part of the audience and most of the content is pitched at children, so a tenth of the children's benefit at most.

rows.label: Mortality benefits as a share of the earnings benefit
rows.explainer: 0 (0-2%): Akili and Me teaches handwashing and healthy habits (a before-after study found children's health knowledge rose, Kauffman and others 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9140413/), but no study links the shows to deaths averted; the health knowledge is counted in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: 0.55 (0.3-0.85), internal × external. Internal 0.6: both effects come from comparisons of children who chose to watch with those who didn't, who may differ; the meta-analysis's studies are small and tested on what the show taught (letters, counting), and small education studies find about three times the effect of large ones (Evans and Yuan 2022, https://doi.org/10.3102/01623737221079646, the source of @education.learning_gain_sd_median_rct_lmic); Ubongo's Nigeria study found no difference by assignment. Against that, Sesame Street experiments find more than its surveys (0.377 against 0.262, Mares & Pan Table 4). External 0.9: Sesame Street's co-productions are, like Akili and Me, local-language curricula broadcast free in poor countries; the Ubongo Kids figure is Ubongo's own audience. Fade-out before adult life is in the shared persistence figure, not here.

rows.label: Share of counted child viewers who watch regularly, like the surveys' viewers
rows.explainer: Judgment 55% (30-80%): a household counts if it tuned in during the month, while the surveys' viewers watched a broadcast season (Akili and Me) or in the past week (Ubongo Kids). Anchors: Ubongo's fact sheet counted 'over 24 million learners' who view or listen regularly, from media ratings of about 2021 (https://www.ubongo.org/wp-content/uploads/Reach_popup.pdf); with watch_share this gives about 15 million regular viewers, 7-24 million across both ranges, the high end Ubongo's own claim. An independent check: Uwezo's 2017 survey found 16.7% of Tanzanian children aged 6-16 had watched Ubongo Kids in the past week, 2.6 million children (Watson, p. 202). Gains rise with engagement: in Ubongo's Nigeria study each Akili and Me character a child could name went with about 3% higher literacy and numeracy scores (Borzekowski and others 2023, Table 2, p. 10), so occasional viewers gain less.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 90% (70-100%): the studies' effects are against children watching other programmes or none, so another channel's cartoons are already netted out; a little educational content (other local or dubbed shows) would fill some of the airtime without Ubongo.

rows.label: Ubongo International's share of the Ubongo group's spending
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (60-100%): the audience is reached by the whole Ubongo group (Ubongo International in the US, Ubongo Learning in Tanzania, offices in Kenya and Rwanda); the US return funds its sister organisations with grants ($3.5 million in 2024), but they also take some grants and earn some content and licensing income of their own. No published account totals the group's 2024 spending; the last group accounts that do, for 2019 (Annual Report 2019, p. 25: expenses $1,278,536), show sales, licensing and co-production as about 5% of revenue, the rest grants and donations, which now flow mostly through Ubongo International. 85% if the African entities spend about $1.3 million a year of their own on top of the US grants; low 60% if they raise a large share themselves.

rows.label: Ubongo's share of the resources behind the broadcasts (against broadcasters' and partners' own)
rows.explainer: Judgment 70% (40-100%), Convention 2: over 60 TV and radio stations carry the shows, free to viewers (Strategic Plan, p. 21; Reach_popup.pdf); Ubongo publishes no airtime terms, and its return shows only $103,139 of advertising and $1.59 million of other fees for services in its programme expenses (Part IX line 11g), which may include airtime bought. Where stations give the airtime, its value counts on the partners' side; partners who run screenings and hand out toolkits give their own time too. 70% if partners' airtime and time are worth about 40% of Ubongo's own spending; 100% if Ubongo pays for all the airtime; 40% if donated airtime is worth one and a half times its spending.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Ubongo International's share of the group's spending × the group's share of everyone's resources behind the broadcasts.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: 0.85 (0.6-1.0): in 2024 Ubongo International raised $29.1 million in grants against $7.2 million of spending, and its net assets rose from $10.1 million to $32.0 million (Form 990, Part I lines 8, 18, 20-22), largely multi-year grants for the 2024-28 plan, whose five-year fundraising goal was $28 million (Strategic Plan, p. 31). With the plan largely funded, part of a new gift is money its large funders would have given anyway. Pledged grants receivable rose from $1.6 million to $20.3 million (Part X line 3); this adjustment carries those committed funds, so the wait before a gift is spent (gift_to_grant_years) counts cash only and isn't lengthened for them too.

rows.label: Cash at the end of 2024

source.title: Ubongo International, Form 990 for 2024 (IRS e-file, via ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer)
source.page: Part X lines 1 and 2, column B
source.quote: Cash non-interest-bearing 11,480,602; savings and temporary cash investments 286,133

rows.explainer: Cash and savings at the year end; pledged grants not yet received are left out, as they aren't money waiting to be spent. Investment income was $6,351 (Part VIII), too little to grow the waiting money.

rows.label: Years a gift waits before it is spent
rows.explainer: Cash at the year end over a year's spending, about {{row:gift_to_grant_years}} years.

rows.label: Discount for the wait before a gift is spent
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate; the wait from viewing to adult earnings is in ln_gain_per_person.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin (the shared missing-data step): Ubongo's household count, with Akili and Me's effect from Sesame Street's studies (other delivery) and Ubongo Kids' from a cross-sectional survey, not a controlled evaluation; Ubongo's own trials publish no standard deviations to pool.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: A side effect, judgment 0 (-10% to +10%): health learning not on the studies' tests (Akili and Me's lessons on handwashing; Kauffman and others 2022 found gains, before-after only, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9140413/), +5%; less the time a child spends in front of a screen instead of playing, reading or being read to, which observational studies link to slower early development, -5%. Social-emotional learning is in the pooled effect already. Either can outweigh.
